content: Pravastatin catalyzes the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, which represents an early and rate-limiting step in the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway. Additionally, pravastatin reduces very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) and triglycerides (TG) levels while increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). Pravastatin sodium, marketed as Pravastatin®, belongs to the statin class of lipid-lowering agents that inhibit cholesterol biosynthesis. These compounds act as competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme responsible for catalyzing the early rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis, specifically the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Chemically, pravastatin sodium is designated as 1-Naphthalene-heptanoic acid, 1,2,6,7,8,8a-hexahydro-β,δ,6-trihydroxy-2-methyl-8-(2-methyl-1-oxobutoxy)-, monosodium salt. Pravastatin sodium is an odorless, white to off-white, fine or crystalline powder. It is highly soluble in methanol and water (greater than 300 mg/mL), slightly soluble in isopropanol, and practically insoluble in acetone, acetonitrile, chloroform, and ether. Pravastatin is available for oral administration in tablet forms of 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, and 80 mg. The inactive ingredients in these tablets include croscarmellose sodium, lactose, magnesium oxide, magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, and povidone. Additionally, the 10 mg tablet contains Red Ferric Oxide, the 20 mg and 80 mg tablets contain Yellow Ferric Oxide, and the 40 mg tablet contains Green Lake Blend (a mixture of D&C Yellow No. 10-Aluminum Lake and FD&C Blue No. 1-Aluminum Lake). The FDA package insert for pravastatin does not provide specific information regarding its pharmacodynamics. Pravastatin is administered orally in its active form. Following oral administration, the average absorption of pravastatin is approximately 34%, with an absolute bioavailability of 17%, as determined by urinary recovery of the total radiolabeled drug. The presence of food in the gastrointestinal tract reduces systemic bioavailability; however, the lipid-lowering effects of the drug remain consistent whether taken with food or one hour before meals. Plasma concentrations of pravastatin, including the area under the concentration-time curve (AUC), maximum concentration (Cmax), and steady-state minimum concentration (Cmin), are directly proportional to the administered dose. Systemic bioavailability is reduced by 60% when pravastatin is administered at bedtime compared to a morning dose. Despite this reduction, the efficacy of pravastatin taken once daily in the evening is marginally more effective than a morning dose, although the difference is not statistically significant. The coefficient of variation (CV) for AUC, based on inter-subject variability, ranges from 50% to 60%. Steady-state AUCs, Cmax, and Cmin plasma concentrations show no evidence of pravastatin accumulation following onceor twice-daily administration of pravastatin tablets. Approximately 50% of circulating pravastatin is bound to plasma proteins. The primary metabolic pathways for pravastatin include (a) isomerization to 6-epi pravastatin and the 3α-hydroxy isomer of pravastatin (SQ 31,906) and (b) enzymatic ring hydroxylation to SQ 31,945. The 3α-hydroxy isomeric metabolite (SQ 31,906) exhibits only 1/10 to 1/40 of the HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity of the parent compound.
